title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
summary: From the natural O(n²) DP recurrence to the O(n log n) patience-sorting optimization — a problem that teaches you two entirely different state representations for the same question.

slides.markdown:
Longest Increasing Subsequence asks: what's the longest subsequence of an array that's strictly increasing, where the elements don't need to be contiguous?

It's a favorite interview problem for a specific reason — there are two genuinely different correct solutions with different complexities, and moving from one to the other requires re-representing the state entirely, not just tweaking a loop. The O(n²) DP is the natural first answer; the O(n log n) patience-sorting trick is the follow-up that separates candidates who've internalized the pattern from those reciting a memorized solution.

Both are worth knowing cold, because interviewers routinely ask for the DP first and then ask "can you do better?"

slides.subTitle: dp[i] = longest chain ending exactly at i
slides.markdown:
Define `dp[i]` as the length of the longest increasing subsequence that **ends exactly at index `i`** — not "using the first `i` elements," but specifically terminating there. That precision matters and is the topic's first pitfall later on.

To compute `dp[i]`, look at every earlier index `j < i`. If `nums[j] < nums[i]`, then extending that chain to include `nums[i]` gives a valid chain of length `dp[j] + 1`. Take the best such extension over all valid `j`, or `1` if no earlier element is smaller (the chain of just `nums[i]` alone):

`dp[i] = max(dp[j] + 1 for all j < i where nums[j] < nums[i])`, or `1` if no such `j` exists.

The answer to the whole problem is `max(dp)` over every index — the longest chain might end anywhere, not necessarily at the last element.

slides.sectionTitle: 'Ending at i' vs. 'using the first i'
slides.markdown:
A very common confusion: reading `dp[i]` as "the LIS length among the first `i` elements" instead of its actual definition, "the LIS length of a chain that ends exactly at index `i`."

Those are different recurrences. "Using the first `i` elements" would just be a running max and wouldn't need to look at `nums[j] < nums[i]` at all — it collapses the problem instead of solving it. The whole reason `dp[i]` is defined as "ending at `i`" is so the recurrence can ask "can I extend a chain that stopped at some earlier `j`" — which requires knowing exactly where a chain ends, not just how long the best chain so far is.

This distinction resurfaces in nearly every 1D DP problem indexed by position: always double-check whether your state means "ending at" or "using up to," because the two support entirely different recurrences.

To recover the actual elements (not just the length), keep a parallel `prev[i]` array recording which earlier index each `dp[i]` extended from. After filling the table, find the index with the max `dp` value and walk backward through `prev` pointers to rebuild the chain in reverse.

![Backward prev-pointer arrows from the index with the maximum dp value chaining back to the start of the increasing subsequence](assets/lis-reconstruct-prev-pointers.svg)

assets.alt: Backward prev-pointer arrows from the index with the maximum dp value chaining back to the start of the increasing subsequence

slides.markdown:
Patience sorting reframes LIS entirely: instead of a table indexed by position, keep an array `tails` where `tails[k]` is the **smallest possible tail value** of any increasing chain of length `k+1` found so far.

Why the smallest tail matters: a smaller tail value is always at least as useful for future extension as a larger one — any element that could extend a chain ending in a larger value can also extend a chain of the same length ending in a smaller value. So `tails` only needs to remember the best (smallest) tail per chain length, discarding every other chain of that length as strictly dominated.

The final answer is simply the length of `tails` once every element has been processed — no need to look at the actual values in it unless you also want the subsequence.

The name comes from a literal card game: deal cards one at a time onto piles, placing each card on the leftmost pile whose current top is >= the card (or starting a new pile if none qualifies). The number of piles at the end equals the LIS length.

![Cards dealt onto piles by top-card value, with one replacing a pile's top and one starting a new pile on the right](assets/lis-patience-piles.svg)

Each pile's top card corresponds to one entry in the `tails` array — the smallest tail seen so far for a chain of that pile's length.

assets.alt: Cards dealt onto piles by top-card value, with one replacing a pile's top and one starting a new pile on the right

slides.markdown:
The single most common mistake with the O(n log n) version: reading `tails` as if it holds the actual longest increasing subsequence. It doesn't — it only tracks the smallest tail achievable for each chain length, and elements can be overwritten by later, unrelated values that happen to form a shorter tail for the same length.

`tails`'s **length** is correct — that genuinely equals the LIS length. Its **contents**, read as a sequence, are usually not a valid increasing subsequence that ever existed in the input in that combination. If you need the actual subsequence, not just its length, you need the `prev`-pointer reconstruction from the O(n²) DP version instead — the patience-sorting version trades away easy reconstruction for speed.

slides.sectionTitle: O(n²) DP vs. O(n log n) patience sorting
slides.markdown:
| | O(n²) DP | O(n log n) patience sorting |
|---|---|---|
| State | dp[i]: chain length ending at i | tails[k]: smallest tail of a length-(k+1) chain |
| Per-element cost | Scan all earlier elements: O(n) | Binary search over tails: O(log n) |
| Reconstructs subsequence easily | Yes, via prev pointers | No — tails isn't the actual chain |
| Mental model | "Extend the best chain ending at each earlier point" | "Keep the most extensible tail per chain length" |

Same final answer (the length), completely different state representation. This pairing is a good template for the broader lesson: sometimes the faster algorithm isn't a tweak to the slower one's code — it's a genuinely different way of describing what's being tracked.

Swap "strictly increasing" for "non-decreasing" and only the binary search function changes — use `bisect_right` instead of `bisect_left` so equal values extend a chain instead of replacing a tail, since ties are now allowed to continue the sequence.

Russian Doll Envelopes (nest envelope A inside B if both dimensions strictly increase) reduces to 2D LIS: sort by width ascending, and for equal widths sort by height **descending** — the descending tie-break prevents two same-width envelopes from being counted as nestable inside each other — then run ordinary 1D LIS on the height sequence alone. Recognizing that a 2D-looking constraint collapses to 1D LIS after the right sort is the pattern to carry forward.
